CO Flux Extraction

Extract and measure carbon monoxide (CO) line fluxes from spectral data cubes. This specialized tool analyzes CO emission or absorption across multiple rotational transitions.

Starting CO Flux Extraction

Access Tool

  1. Click HITRAN menu in toolbar

  2. Input min/max wavelengths and click on HITRAN button

  3. Choose molecule, isotopologue number, and vibrational level

  4. (Optionally) Refresh HITRAN query

The spectrum now shows the lines given those parameters. Hovering over a line shows its species, its wavelength, its transition, and its Einstein coefficients You can remove a line by clicking on it in the spectrum or by clicking on the SPECIES button which renders a table with all the current species.

Load Contaminating Lines

Additionally (and optionally), you can load a catalog of contaminating (non-target) lines so both CO Flux Map and Multi-Gaussian Fit (below) can account for them instead of letting their flux distort a nearby CO line’s measurement.

  1. Click on Load Contaminating Lines and load a .csv file with unwanted lines

IMPORTANT: Make sure this file has a column called ‘wavelength’.

Loading the catalog doesn’t retroactively update results you’ve already produced – run CO Flux Map / Multi-Gaussian Fit again after loading it for the fit to pick it up.

Multi-Gaussian Fit

Fit every currently-plotted HITRAN line at once via linear least squares. Each line’s center is fixed at its catalog wavelength, and its width comes from the instrument’s own spectral resolution rather than being fitted – these lines are instrumentally unresolved, so width is a property of the instrument, not something to estimate per line or per fit. With both fixed, solving for every line’s amplitude becomes a single linear solve instead of an iterative nonlinear one: no risk of a weak line’s fit window drifting off it, and overlapping lines are disentangled correctly because they’re all solved for together rather than one at a time. fit_hitran_lines() in cube_explorer.api runs this exact algorithm (see Using the API below); it is not an approximation of the GUI button, the two share the same code path.

If you’ve loaded a contaminating-lines catalog (above), any contaminant that falls in the fitted range and is far enough from every requested line (at least ~2σ) gets its own component too, so its flux is absorbed there instead of leaking into a nearby CO line’s amplitude. It’s drawn as a green outline on the plot and listed separately in the results – never counted toward the CO line total. A contaminant too close to a requested line to reliably tell the two apart (<2σ) isn’t given its own component; that CO line’s result gets a note instead, flagging the unresolved nearby contaminant rather than reporting an unreliable split.

  1. Perform automatic continuum on the 1D spectrum by clicking on Continuum Tools → Automatic Continuum → Continuum Line

  2. Click on Multi-Gaussian Fit

A Gaussian curve is overlaid on the spectrum for each plotted line, and a results window opens with one block per line, plus a separate section listing any contaminating lines that got their own component.

Reading the results

Each line’s block reports two groups of numbers:

  • Catalog identification — Line λ, Transition, A coeff and E_upper, copied straight from the HITRAN entry, not measured. Useful for cross-checking that the fit actually locked onto the line you think it did.

  • Fitted parameters — Center, Amplitude, Sigma, FWHM, Integrated Area and R². Center is always exactly the catalog wavelength – it’s fixed, not fitted – and Sigma follows the instrument’s spectral resolution rather than varying line to line the way a free nonlinear fit’s would. Units follow the same rules as the 1D page (1D Spectrum Fitting) — Integrated Area is erg/s/cm² wherever the header supports the conversion.

A CONTAMINATING LINES section follows the fitted lines whenever any contaminant got its own component: wavelength, species, amplitude and area for each – these are not part of the CO line count or total above.

Using the API

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, fit_hitran_lines
from cube_explorer.line_catalog import load_contaminating_lines_catalog

cube = load_cube("data.fits")
contam = load_contaminating_lines_catalog("path/to/ContaminatingLines.csv")  # optional

results = fit_hitran_lines(
    wavelength=cube.wavelength,
    spectrum=cube.spectrum,
    molecule='CO',
    wavelength_min=4.40,
    wavelength_max=4.80,
    v_upper=1,              # v=1->0, same filter as the HITRAN dialog
    v_lower=0,
    header=cube.header,     # Required for the erg/s/cm2 conversion
    wave_unit=cube.wave_unit,
    contam_catalog=contam,  # omit (or None) to skip contaminant handling entirely
)

detected = [r for r in results if r['success']]
print(f"Fitted {len(detected)}/{len(results)} lines")
for r in sorted(detected, key=lambda r: r['wavelength']):
    print(f"  {r['wavelength']:.6f} um  area={r['area']:.4e} {r['area_unit']}  R2={r['r_squared']:.4f}")

Fitted 56/56 lines
  4.402678 um  area=1.0164e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.3553
  4.407041 um  area=1.2351e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.8765
  4.411493 um  area=1.9398e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.8866
  ...
  4.773583 um  area=6.2902e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.8193
  4.783296 um  area=5.7530e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.5895
  4.793124 um  area=5.8123e-16 erg/s/cm²  R2=0.6617

This reproduces the worked example above exactly: fitted centers, areas and R² match the screenshot’s results window to the last reported digit, because it is the same fit (fit_hitran_lines is what the GUI button calls). Contaminating lines from contam that got their own component aren’t in results at all – they exist purely to keep the CO lines’ amplitudes honest; if you need their values too, they’re only currently exposed through the GUI’s results text, not this return value.

Important

As with fit_line, pass header/wave_unit to get area in erg/s/cm² — without them it stays in the cube’s native units, and area_unit always tells you which one you got. There is no continuum-fitting step in the example above because none was given: leaving continuum unset fits one automatically with fit_continuum(), the same fallback the GUI uses when you have not run Automatic Continuum interactively. Pass your own continuum array to use a continuum you already fitted instead.

Analyze CO for All Pixels

Extract a CO flux map across every spatial pixel:

  1. Click on CO Flux Map.

  2. A popup explains that continuum subtraction runs automatically per pixel, using default parameters that work well for typical spectra. Click No to use those defaults, or Yes to open the same parameter dialog as the manual Automatic Continuum tool and set your own values instead.

  3. A preview shows the brightest pixel within your wavelength range, with the (deduplicated) HITRAN lines marked – a sanity check before committing to a full-cube run. Click YES - Extract Map to proceed.

If you’ve already run an extraction with the same wavelength range and continuum choice, you’ll be offered the cached results instead of re-running.

Progress Monitoring

The progress dialog updates per pixel as the cube is processed.

Output Products

  • CO Flux Map: integrated flux per pixel

  • Detection Count: number of lines detected per pixel

  • Export as FITS / Show Statistics buttons in the results window

Inspecting Individual Pixels

With Pixel Select on (the default), clicking a pixel on either map opens that pixel’s fit:

Turn Pixel Select off to zoom/pan the map freely instead of reopening this dialog on every click.

Using the CO Flux API

Extract CO fluxes programmatically for single spectra or full data cubes, using extract_co_flux() and create_co_flux_map() – the same algorithm as the GUI’s CO Flux Map button.

Note

This is a different algorithm from Multi-Gaussian Fit / fit_hitran_lines() above, not a scripted version of it, and the two don’t produce identical totals for the same spectrum – expect them to land within roughly 10-20%, not match exactly. extract_co_flux/create_co_flux_map fit every line in a 0.1 µm wavelength chunk simultaneously against one shared local continuum, via nonlinear least squares (curve_fit), and only count a line if it clears a per-pixel signal-to-noise threshold first (snr_threshold, default 3σ). fit_hitran_lines fits every requested line at once via linear least squares with fixed centers/widths, with no SNR gate at all – it fits whatever you selected, weak lines included.

The gap between the two is usually dominated by that SNR gate, not a disagreement about the underlying signal: CO Flux Map fits pixel-by-pixel, and a real but weak line often can’t clear 3σ in any single noisy pixel, so it contributes nothing to that pixel’s flux. fit_hitran_lines fits one combined, much higher-SNR spectrum directly, so it can recover that same real flux. Summed over many pixels this adds up to CO Flux Map running systematically lower. Lowering snr_threshold narrows the gap, but that’s trading a real problem (missing weak, real flux) for a different one (counting noise as detections) – it isn’t a way to make either number more correct, just a way to make them agree.

Extract CO Flux from a Single Spectrum

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, extract_co_flux

cube = load_cube("data.fits")

co_result = extract_co_flux(
    wavelength=cube.wavelength,
    spectrum=cube.spectrum,
    co_catalog_path="path/to/CO_catalog.ecsv",
    header=cube.header,      # Required for the erg/s/cm2 conversion
    wave_unit=cube.wave_unit,
)

print(f"Total CO flux: {co_result['co_flux']:.4e} {co_result['flux_unit']}")
print(f"Number of lines detected: {len(co_result['detected_lines'])}")
print(f"Mean continuum level: {co_result['mean_continuum']:.3f}")

Important

As with fit_line/fit_hitran_lines, pass header/wave_unit to get co_flux/contam_flux in erg/s/cm2 – without them they stay in the cube’s native units, and flux_unit always tells you which one you got. Continuum subtraction runs automatically (subtract_continuum=True by default, same defaults as the GUI’s Automatic Continuum) – there’s no need to pre-subtract it yourself. Pass your own continuum_params dict to override those defaults, e.g. continuum_params={'window_size': 101}.

Create CO Flux Maps

Generate flux maps for the entire data cube:

from cube_explorer.api import load_cube, create_co_flux_map

cube = load_cube("data.fits")

# Uses HITRAN automatically by default, or pass co_catalog_path for a custom catalog
co_flux_map = create_co_flux_map(
    cube,
    wavelength_min=4.70, wavelength_max=4.80,
    n_jobs=4,
)

print(f"CO flux map shape: {co_flux_map['flux_map'].shape}, unit: {co_flux_map['flux_unit']}")
print(f"Mean CO flux: {co_flux_map['flux_map'][co_flux_map['flux_map'] > 0].mean():.4e}")
print(f"Pixels with CO detection: {(co_flux_map['detection_map'] > 0).sum()}")

Continuum subtraction works the same way as extract_co_flux above – automatic per pixel, with the default parameters unless you pass your own via continuum_params. There’s no separate header argument here since cube (and its header) is already the first argument; the erg/s/cm2 conversion is attempted automatically, and flux_unit tells you whether it succeeded.

Expected Catalog Format

The CO catalog file should be in ECSV (Enhanced Character Separated Values) format with columns:

  • line_wave_um: Wavelength in micrometers

  • species: Molecule name (e.g., “CO”)

  • transition: Transition description (e.g., “v=1->0, J=4->5”)

  • a: Einstein A coefficient

Columns are loaded as-is, with no validation – a file missing line_wave_um or species won’t fail at load time, only later inside the fit, as a KeyError.

Tips for CO Flux Extraction

  • Ensure your wavelength calibration is accurate (errors affect line identification)

  • The algorithm automatically measures line widths and integrates flux

  • For more control over individual line fits, use fit_hitran_lines() instead
